title: Your balance
hook: worship, work, rest and family: give each its right (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, khidmah. Your line: serve. Did you do one helpful thing for someone who couldn't thank you? A school, a teacher, a mosque, a circle, a gift, a trait, a family, a neighbor, service. That is a lot to carry. Today, how to carry it. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

Salman comes to visit his friend Abu al-Darda and finds Abu al-Darda's wife in shabby, careless clothes. What's wrong? he asks. Your brother, she says, has no interest in this world. Abu al-Darda comes in, puts food in front of his guest, and says: eat, I'm fasting. Salman says: I won't eat unless you eat. So he eats. That night Abu al-Darda gets up to pray, and Salman tells him: sleep. Later he gets up again. Sleep, says Salman. Near the end of the night, Salman wakes him, and the two of them pray together. Then Salman says the line Sahih al-Bukhari keeps. Today, worship, work, rest and family: giving each its right.
screen: `A WIFE IN SHABBY CLOTHES.` → `EAT. SLEEP.` → `THEN THEY PRAY TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the line. Your Lord has a right over you, your own self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give each one its right. When they told the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, what had happened, he said: Salman has spoken the truth. Next, notice who was out of balance. Not a lazy man. A devout one, fasting through the day and rising to pray through the night, while his wife sat in shabby clothes. Too much of a good thing had pushed something else out. Third, the same correction, told another way. In another report in Bukhari, the Prophet hears that the companion Abdullah ibn Amr fasts every day and prays every night. He tells him: fast and break your fast, pray and sleep, for your body has a right over you, your eyes have a right over you, and your wife has a right over you. Eyes have a right. Sleep is not a lapse in devotion. It's owed. Fourth, why it holds together. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." A practice that breaks the person practicing it isn't what was asked. Last, the whole block. Over these weeks you've met a diverse ummah, asked the questions of today, and built a practice for today, one piece at a time. Balance is what keeps all of it standing. Not everything every day. Each thing its right.
screen: `GIVE EACH ONE ITS RIGHT.` · `A DEVOUT MAN, OUT OF BALANCE.` · `YOUR EYES HAVE A RIGHT.` · `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: The practice: rest well tonight. Begin it now. Sit back and let your breath slow down without forcing it. Go through the four rights one at a time, and give each a breath. Worship: where it has a place in your day, or a place you'd like it to have. Work: what it asked of you today. Family: one face, one need. And yourself: your body, your eyes, how tired they are. Notice which of the four got crowded out this week. No blame. Just notice. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the day in your own words. Then plan one thing for tonight: a screen off earlier, a lighter evening, a proper bedtime. The bell holds the time.
Your balance. Giving your Lord, yourself, your family and your work each their right, so none crowds out the rest. Today's word.

Your line: give each its right. Tonight, let your eyes have theirs: go to bed on time. This block ends here. Tomorrow the year starts gathering itself in: the pillars, reviewed. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of Salman and Abu al-Darda, 'give each one its right', as a guide to balancing worship, work, rest and family, so that devotion does not crowd out sleep, health or the rights of a spouse and children.

fork.setup: you're Salman, visiting your friend. he's fasting, he keeps rising to pray through the night, and his wife is in shabby clothes. what do you do?
options: praise his devotion and leave him to it.
tell him to eat and sleep, and give each one its right.
fork.reveal: Salman made him eat, told him to sleep, prayed with him near the end of the night, and said give each one its right. the Prophet said Salman had spoken the truth (Sahih al-Bukhari).

original.note: Arabic: a right, something owed; also truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: balance means doing a little less religion.
what it means: giving your Lord, yourself, your family and your body each their right, so devotion doesn't crowd out the rest.
what a scholar hears: Salman's words to Abu al-Darda confirmed by the Prophet, the correction of Abdullah ibn Amr, and al-Baqarah: not beyond its scope.

sources.quoted: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.

notes: Confirm Sahih al-Bukhari 1968 for the Salman and Abu al-Darda story and the paraphrase of its details (Umm al-Darda's clothes, the meal, waking to pray near the end of the night).
Confirm Sahih al-Bukhari 1975 for the Abdullah ibn Amr report (body, eyes and wife each have a right).
The outline hook lists 'worship, work, rest and family'; the hadith itself names the Lord, the self and the family. The script keeps work from the outline; check.

Editor: the teach and fork said Abu al-Darda fasted 'every day' and prayed 'all night', which Sahih al-Bukhari 1968 does not state (it shows him fasting that day and rising at night; 'fasts every day' belongs to the Abdullah ibn Amr report); reworded in the teach, match and fork, and 'his wife quietly stopped caring how she looked' now keeps to the report's shabby clothes.
Camp end: the teach names the block's three parts (a diverse ummah, questions of today, a practice for today) and the carry points to the year-four close.
